lines.text: Your king wants the biggest ship the world has ever seen.
So you haul timber from Mount Etna, enough, ancient writers say, for sixty warships.
Three hundred craftsmen raise the ribs, and in six months half the hull is done.
Inside, you stack three gangways: cargo, thirty cabins, and soldiers on top.
But a hull this huge must hold together at sea.
So you pin it with bronze rivets, many weighing ten pounds.
Then you wrap it in tarred linen and sheets of lead.
But the giant is stuck on land, and no crew can push it.
So Archimedes rigs a windlass, and it slides into the sea. This is the Syracusia.
On top, ancient writers say, you add a gymnasium, gardens, and grapevines growing in casks of earth.
A shrine to Aphrodite with an agate floor, a library, and a bath with three bronze tubs.
Twenty horse stalls, a freshwater tank, and a fish tank lined with lead.
But a floating palace is a target, so you raise eight towers full of archers.
And Archimedes builds a machine that hurls a hundred and eighty pound stone. This is a catapult.
But the bilge fills with water.
So one man pumps it out with a turning screw. This is an Archimedes screw.
But harbors can't safely take a ship this big.
So the king renames her Alexandris, fills her with grain, and sends her to Egypt as a gift.
Congratulations. You have built a giant ship.
